title: Gorse and Halo's Lost Rosette
markdown:
Moonbeams stitched silver through the stable windows. Outside, the night kept its voice down. Gorse the guinea pig, moss-coloured after rain, twitched a worry in his whiskers. Tonight was the grand stable celebration: warm apple cider, songs that fitted together, fairy lights like captured stars. His bright blue rosette—robin’s-egg bright, morning-kissed—was not in any of the places it liked.

“Oh dear,” he whispered, a squeak in the deep quiet. He wiggled his nose as if willpower were a magnet. The rosette declined. “Where could it be?”

A nuzzle warmer than a summer breeze found his side. Halo the horse stood there, coat like creamy moonlight, mane a river of silk, eyes with the patience of old trees. “What troubles you, little friend?” Her voice was low thunder on a far hill, the comfortable kind.

Gorse explained, trembling no more than a leaf in a polite wind. “The celebration is soon. It was right here. I am sure.”

Halo lowered her great head; velvet nose brushed his ear. “We shall find it. The stable is quiet. We will look in every nook, without hurrying the straw.” The moon came along as a silver guide. Their steps stayed soft.

They ambled past slumbering sheep, woolly clouds that only sighed and misted the air. Halo asked a ewe very politely; the ewe dreamed of clover and did not file a report. They checked the grain bin’s shadow, the empty bucket, the fold of a horse-blanket that had ideas about being a hiding place and was not. No blue. A moth-wing of unease opened in Gorse’s chest. Stars climbed past the window bars. The rosette did not appear to cheer him.

“Perhaps it rolled under a stone. Or into a hollow. Or a sheep borrowed it for a dream.” His paws shuffled, paper-soft in the straw.

Halo’s breath smelled of sweet hay and ruffled him. “Patience. Try the old oak at the meadow’s edge. Lost things sometimes sit where the wind tells secrets and the light is gentle enough to read by.”

They meandered through tall grass that danced in its sleep. In the dew-kissed clover they found Caradoc the badger, earthy browns and greys, sorting a tangle of ribbons spread like a fallen rainbow.

“Good evening, Caradoc,” Halo said. “Have you seen a small bright blue rosette? Gorse has misplaced his, and the celebration is near.”

Caradoc paused, a long silken blue ribbon the colour of summer sky in his paws. “A rosette. I have blues and golds and silvers, all waiting their turn.” Kind pebble-eyes found Gorse. “What makes yours special?”

Gorse thought of Mrs. Higgins, the farmer’s wife, and the spectacles that lived on her nose until they didn’t. He had helped find them. Friends had cheered. Pride had been a warm room. The blue had seemed to hold a piece of that summer sky.

“It reminds me of kindness,” he said, stronger, a stream over stones. “And of happy moments.”

Caradoc nodded, slow. “Then it already holds a story. Looking sometimes shows other things, even before the thing itself sits up.”

Lighter, still rosette-less, they went deeper into the meadow, Halo’s hooves careful so as not to flatten a clue. Fireflies blinked like fallen stars with poor aim. They searched under broad leaves, around the gnarled roots of wildflowers, and along a ditch that kept only a frog’s opinion. Dewdrops on webs, diamond-bright, and a gold ribbon Caradoc had missed, which they carried back to his pile because that was the sort of night it was. Not the prize. A gentle sadness misted in from the hills. The celebration felt like a tune in another building, cider warming for someone else.

They turned back along the moonlit path, grass rustling, breath quiet. Gorse’s whiskers drooped. He had still had Halo, and Caradoc’s ribbons, and the walk. That was a kind of pocket.

At the stable door Halo paused. “Wait.” Her eyes fixed on a cozy bale of sweet hay in the far corner, a little stack that invited sitting. She nudged it, encouraging as a blanket pulled up.

Underneath, peeking like a shy blue flower in gold, lay the rosette, safe, undisturbed, as if the hay had been keeping a secret for someone patient. A wisp of straw wore it like a joke. Gorse squeaked relief, a happy sound that the rafters kept, and picked it up in his teeth. It still held a little of this morning’s sun, and a little of the celebration that had not started without him.

Moonlight caught the shimmer. He looked at Halo, a blanket of a friend, and at the ribbon-memory of the meadow. The fabric was lovely. The search had been a second prize that did not need pinning.

He set the rosette beside him on the straw and snuggled to Halo’s warm flank. Hay-sweet. Breathing in two sizes, a lullaby without words. The celebration would have cider and music. This corner, for a minute, was enough.

Gorse yawned, a secret the night agreed to keep. Halo rested her chin near him. Stars showed through the door, tiny sleepy eyes. They drifted off with the rosette where it could be found in the morning without another quest, which was, Gorse decided in the last clear thought, a kindness too.
